texts.preview: Today, we look at personalized news feeds and the way they shape what people see each day. These feeds can make it easier to find relevant stories, but they also raise questions about what may stay out of view and who decides what matters. By the end, you will understand the main question behind this experience: how much should a news feed choose for us?
texts.comment_1: Listen for two different ways of looking at the same experience.
texts.comment_2: To explore that question, let’s hear from two different voices. Each person will speak from their own point of view.
texts.comment_3: Instead of deciding which voice is right, let’s ask a different question: Why can the same kind of feed feel different to different people? The next part looks more closely at that question.
texts.comment_4: So the question is not only which reader is right. It is also what makes each person’s experience possible, including the choices and limits they face. That takes us one step deeper than the disagreement itself.

flagged_items.quoted_evidence: In an analysis of more than ten million US users, feed ranking reduced exposure to different political sides, though users’ own clicks played an even larger role. During the election period studied, like-minded sources made up most of what active adults saw.
